summary:
Moldova's anti-discrimination statute, Law No. 2 of 2023, names gender identity and, separately, sexual orientation among grounds protected from "any kind of discrimination". An employment discrimination ban covering sexual orientation has been in force since 1 January 2013, and Article 11 of the audiovisual media code, effective 1 January 2019, prohibits broadcasting incitement to hatred founded on intolerance, including on grounds of sexual orientation. Hate speech and hate crimes have been criminal offences since 2022 with both grounds named, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover them. Consensual sex between men has been legal since 1995 and the age of consent was equalised in 2002. ILGA-Europe ranked Moldova last among 49 European countries for LGBT legislation in 2012 and 23rd by 2023.

Transgender people in Moldova may change their legal name and gender on official documents, but a psychiatric diagnosis confirming "transgenderism" is required to do so.

Enforcement does not match the statutory text. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2024 reports that a trans woman was denied bank service over a mismatch between her documents and her appearance; the Equality Council confirmed the discrimination and recommended preventive measures. The same review found hate speech remained a serious problem with no meaningful state response, a finding echoed in the European Commission's country report, and noted that election-period political hate speech rose. Amnesty International's 2025 reporting states that discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace and that freedom of expression and assembly was arbitrarily restricted, with impunity for past violations.

Society remains markedly unreceptive. The Equality Council study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022", published January 2023, found acceptance of LGBT+ people extremely low: 79% of respondents would not accept LGBT+ neighbours and 60% would not accept them as work colleagues, with marginalisation of LGBT+ people increasing during 2022. The same source states that discrimination and violence against LGBT community members are commonplace and politicians often make derogatory remarks about them.

Public Pride proceeds openly. Participants of all ages and backgrounds joined Moldova Pride 2024 in Chisinau. Police protected marchers at the May 2018 Pride, deploying tear gas on 19 May against anti-LGBT protesters attempting to disrupt the solidarity march. Earlier events were not protected: on 11 May 2008 police and authorities stood by as crowds attacked Pride participants after the mayor banned the parade, and the European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2012 that Moldovan authorities violated human rights by cancelling that event; the May 2017 march was cancelled by police shortly after it started following attacks by fundamentalist Orthodox groups. In May 2019 a human rights lawyer representing GENDERDOC-M suffered an arson attack on her car in central Chisinau and police refused to investigate, saying the damage was not "significant".

Local "gay propaganda" bans enacted in several cities and districts in 2012, including Balti, Drochia, Cahul and Ceadir-Lunga, carried no administrative sanctions. The Balti Court of Appeals ruled on 28 February 2013 that the city's ban was unconstitutional and violated human rights. On 30 April 2013 the Parliament of Gagauzia approved a bill forbidding "propaganda" of homosexuality, bisexuality and transness, with no fines but with provisions banning registration of LGBT-related organisations and banning LGBT-related clubs and entertainment establishments; it was invalidated by court decision on 20 June 2013 for violating freedom of speech and human rights. A 2013 national bill banning "propaganda" of relations outside constitutional marriage was narrowed by a bill passed 11 October 2013 to remove the interpretable content.

In Russian-occupied Transnistria, new legislation prohibits promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations", per Amnesty International's 2025 report.

The Constitution defines marriage as between a man and a woman, with no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions.

A trans detainee's case documents conditions inside the penitentiary system. Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man registered female at birth in 1972 whose documents were changed to male in 2007, served a four-year sentence, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit, supposedly for his own safety, while his request to be placed in the unit for detainees requiring protection was refused. He describes forced strip searches, being called for the gynaecologist over the intercom, staff opening his bathroom door, and being called "Natașa" at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration replied that he was detained alone "at his own written request" with no rights violated and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. Observatorul de Nord corroborated on 7 April 2025 that he spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6, fully isolated and humiliated by staff on grounds of sexual orientation, bringing him to the edge of suicide; the authorities admit homophobia persists in state institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment. The most recent documented instance of this treatment in the record is 2025; no later instance is documented.
tangentialFactors:
ECOM's 2024 legislative analysis on SOGI and HIV in Moldova identifies legal barriers affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV across access to justice, hate-crime provisions and discrimination provisions, benchmarked against international standards and based on a survey of local partners.

In June 2011 Moldova voted against the UN Human Rights Council resolution condemning discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity; that resolution was nonetheless adopted on 17 June 2011 by 23 votes to 19, establishing a formal UN process to document abuses including discriminatory laws and acts of violence against LGBT people.

A Ministry of Health official letter states that homosexuality is not considered a disease and that medical services are accessible regardless of sexual orientation.

ILGA-Europe's ranking movement from last of 49 in 2012 to 23rd in 2023 reflects legislative expansion on sexual orientation and gender identity, and does not by itself measure enforcement or social acceptance, which the Equality Council's 2022 prejudice study and Amnesty's 2025 reporting place at a much lower level.
localsOnly:

The Equality Council confirmed discrimination in the 2024 bank-service denial case involving a trans woman and recommended preventive measures, giving residents a domestic avenue for complaints on document and appearance mismatch grounds.

Authorities state they are training penitentiary staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment following the reporting on conditions at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca.

Local "propaganda" bans enacted in 2012 in Balti, Drochia, Cahul and Ceadir-Lunga carried no administrative sanctions, and the Balti ban was struck down by the Balti Court of Appeals on 28 February 2013; the Gagauzia Parliament's 30 April 2013 bill was invalidated by court decision on 20 June 2013.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the psychiatric-diagnosis requirement for legal gender recognition has been amended since the source snapshot is unresolved in this record.

The ECOM analysis identifies legal barriers affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV but the specific barriers are not itemised in the inventory; the document itself would need to be consulted.

The current enforcement status of the Transnistrian legislation prohibiting promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations", and whether it has been applied to any individual, is not sourced here.

Whether the Equality Council's recommended preventive measures in the bank-denial case were implemented is unresolved.

No trans-specific violence rate with a denominator is available for Moldova in this inventory, so no comparative magnitude of trans-targeted violence against the general homicide rate can be stated.
